title: RDS 2.0 control board, DVT2 hashboards
provenance: Slot counts and populations measured on hardware, not taken from a datasheet: 4 fans from hwmon0..3 paired with pwmchip0..3; 3 hashboard slots from the three 9-bit chain UARTs and three I2C adapters; 100 ASICs per hashboard from the device-initiated DTS/VS stream, where every one of 100 ids contributed exactly 5,429 frames over 27.8 s, measured on hardware.

air-0b.title: air cooled, control board only -- bring-up and harness work

bench.title: not an RDS -- a workstation or CI host running the driver

rules.why: An air-cooled chassis must have every fan it was built with. The fans are the only thing moving heat, there is no redundancy declared for them, and a fan that will not turn is a mechanical or control fault -- not a degraded mode to run in. Free-run is NOT maximum on this chassis (5,430 rpm against 6,800 commanded), so 'do nothing' is not a safe default either.
An immersion chassis has no fans by design. Their absence is the expected shape of the machine, and a tachometer that answers anyway is worth recording but decides nothing.

The machine runs on two boards, or one, or none -- a control board with no hashboard is a legitimate configuration for bring-up and harness work. A fitted board that does not answer is a real finding and must be loud, but it is not a reason to refuse to start: the remaining boards are unaffected and the operator may be expecting it.

A missing device on a board we are driving changes the hashrate we should expect and may be the first sign of a chain fault, so it is loud. It does not block: 99 of 100 devices is a working board, and refusing would make one dead part cost a whole machine.

parent_not_fitted.why: A component whose parent is not fitted in this variant cannot be a fault of this configuration. A failed ASIC on a hashboard we deliberately excluded is interesting -- it is worth knowing before that board is ever fitted -- but it is not actionable now and must never gate a start.
